ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The figure shows an NPN transistor common-collector (emitter follower) circuit. The input voltage source on the left is labeled Vin, connected to the transistor base, and the lower end of the input source is grounded. The transistor collector is connected upward to the +15 V power supply. The transistor emitter node is labeled Vout to the right, and at the same time this emitter node is grounded through a 1.5 kΩ resistor. Reasoning: The problem gives Vin = 0.5 V, and the base-emitter forward voltage required for a standard silicon NPN transistor to conduct is about 0.7 V. If the emitter is initially pulled to 0 V by the pull-down resistor, then the base-emitter voltage VBE = 0.5 V - 0 V = 0.5 V, less than 0.7 V, therefore the base-emitter junction cannot be sufficiently forward biased, and the transistor is cut off. When the transistor is cut off, there is no emitter current supplied by the transistor, and the emitter/output node is pulled to ground potential by the 1.5 kΩ resistor, so the output voltage is 0 V.

With no emitter current supplied by the transistor, the 1.5 kΩ resistor pulls the emitter/output node to 0 V. Output voltage = 0 V.

method.method_draft: First describe the image: the NPN transistor is wired as a common collector, so the output follows the base input at roughly one diode drop lower when on. From the text, substitute Vin = 0.5 V and VBE = 0.7 V into the piecewise emitter-follower rule: Vout = max(0, 0.5 − 0.7) V. Output voltage = 0 V.
